source_text: Καὶ οὐ τὸ μὲν οὕτως ἑστιαθῆναι λαμπρῶς μόνον κερδαίνου σιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς χεῖρας πεπληρωμένας πολυτελῶν δώρων κατάγουσι, καὶ μανθάνουσι παρ' ἡμῶν, ὅτι λυσιτελεῖ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα μετιέναι καὶ πράττειν αὐτοῖς. Εἰ δὲ παρασταίη πένης ἡμῖν, μόλις ὑπὸ τοῦ λιμοῦ καὶ φθεγγόμενος, ἀποστρεφό μεθα τὸν ὁμοφυῆ, βδελυττόμεθα, μετὰ σπουδῆς ἀποτρέχομεν, ὥσπερ δεδοικότες μὴ καὶ τῆς δυσπραγίας αὐτῆς ἐκ τοῦ σχολαίτερον βαδίσαι μετάσχωμεν. Καὶ, εἰ μὲν εἰς γῆν νεύσοι, τὴν συμφορὰν αἰσχυνόμενος, ὑποκρίσεως εἶναι λέγομεν ἐργάτην αὐτόν· εἰ δὲ μετὰ παῤῥησίας προσβλέψοι διὰ τὸ βαρὺ τοῦ λιμοῦ κέν τρον ἡμᾶς, ἀναιδῆ πάλιν καλοῦμεν καὶ βίαιον. Καὶ, εἰ μὲν τύχοι καλυπτόμενος ὑγιέσιν ἐσθήμασιν δεδω κότος τινὸς, ὡς ἄπληστον ἀπελαύνομεν, καὶ ὀμνύμεθα προσποιεῖσθαι πενίαν αὐτόν· εἰ δὲ σκεπάζοιτο σεσηπόσι ῥακίοις, ὡς ὀδωδότα πάλιν διώκομεν, καὶ οὔτε τὸ τοῦ κτίσαντος ὄνομα ταῖς ἱκετηρίαις ἐκεῖνος ἀναμιγνὺς, οὔτε τὸ μὴ τοιούτοις πάθεσι περιπεσεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐξορκῶν συνεχῶς, δύναται τὴν ἀνελεῆ κάμψαι προαίρεσιν. Διὰ ταῦτα ὑφορῶμαι βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος. Εἰ μὲν οὖν ὁ καιρὸς ἐνεδίδου, δύναμίς τε ἀρκοῦσα ὑπῆν, πάντα ἂν ὑμῖν τὰ κατ' ἐκεῖνον, ὅπως ἔδειξεν ἡ Βίβλος, ἐπεξελθὼν ἀπέδωκα τὴν ἐργασίαν τῶν λόγων· νῦν δὲ ὥρα διαφεῖναι πεπονηκότας ὑμᾶς. Αὐτοὶ δὲ εἰ καί τι παραλελοίπαμεν δι' ἀσθένειαν ἐννοίας ἅμα καὶ γλώττης, ἑαυτοῖς ἀναπλάττοντες, ὥσπερ τινὰ φάρμακα τοῖς τῶν ψυχῶν προσαγάγετε τραύμασι. Δίδου γὰρ σοφῷ ἀφορμὴν, καὶ σοφώτερος ἔσται, φησὶν ἡ Γραφή. Δυνατὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς πᾶσαν χάριν περισσεῦσαι εἰς ὑμᾶς, ἵνα, ἐν παντὶ πάντοτε πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν ἔχοντες, περισσεύητε εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἤδη πρὸς λιμένας ἡμῖν, ὡς ὁρᾶτε, καταχθέντα τὸν λόγον, εἰς τὸν τῆς συμβουλῆς δρόμον αὖθις ἀδελφοί τινες ἐπανάγουσι, μὴ παραδραμεῖν τὰ χθὲς ὑπὸ τοῦ Δεσπότου θαυματουργηθέντα κε λεύοντες, μηδὲ σιγῆσαι τὸ τρόπαιον, ὃ κατὰ τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου λύττης ἔστησεν ὁ Σωτήρ· δοῦναι δὲ ἀφορμὴν τῶν τῆς ὑμνῳδίας σκιρτημάτων ὑμῖν. Πάλιν μὲν γὰρ, ὡς ἴστε, τὴν οἰκείαν ὁ διάβολος καθ' ἡμῶν ἐπεδείξατο λύτταν, καὶ φλογὶ πυρὸς ὁπλίσας ἑαυτὸν, τοῖς τῆς Ἐκκλησίας σηκοῖς ἐπεστράτευσε. Πάλιν δὲ ἡ κοινὴ μήτηρ ἐνίκησε, καὶ τῷ πολεμίῳ περιέτρεψε τὸ μηχάνημα, καὶ οὐδὲν ὑπῆρξεν αὐτῷ πλὴν τοῦ δημοσιεῦσαι τὴν ἔχθραν. Ἀντέπνευσεν ἡ χάρις ταῖς τοῦ πολεμίου ῥοπαῖς· ἔμεινεν ὁ νεὼς ἀπαθής. Οὐκ ἴσχυσεν ὁ προσ αχθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ πολεμίου χειμὼν τινάξαι τὴν πέτραν ἐφ' ἧς ὁ Χριστὸς τὴν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ποίμνης ᾠκοδόμησε μάνδραν. Ἐτάχθη καὶ νῦν μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ καὶ πάλαι σβέσας ἐν Βαβυλῶνι τὴν κάμινον. Πῶς οἴεσθε στέ νει σήμερον ὁ διάβολος, οὐκ ἀπολαύσας ἐφ' ᾧπερ ἠβουλήθη τῆς ἐγχειρήσεως; Γείτονα μὲν γὰρ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὁ δυσμενὴς ἀνῆψε πυρὰν, ἵνα ταῖς ἡμετέραις εὐπραγίαις λυμήνηται· καὶ πανταχόθεν ἡ φλὸξ ἀναῤῥιπιζομένη ταῖς βιαίοις ἐκείνου πνοαῖς, ὑπερεχεῖτο τῶν ὑποκειμένων αὐτῇ, καὶ τὸν ἀέρα τὸν ἐγγὺς ἐπενέμετο, ψαῦσαι τῶν ἀνακτόρων ἀναγκαζομένη, καὶ πρὸς κοινωνίαν ἡμᾶς καθέλκουσα τῆς συμφορᾶς. Ὁ Σωτὴρ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν ἀνάψαντα ταύ την ῥυῆναι πεποίηκε, καὶ συστεῖλαι τὴν μανίαν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἑαυτὸν πάλιν προσέταξε.
thought_title: The poor are rejected while flatterers are rewarded; the fire is the devil's defeated assault
orientation: Basil is preaching to his congregation, contrasting their lavish entertainment of flatterers with their harsh rejection of the poor, and then turning to the recent fire outside the church as a defeated attack by the devil.
pass_a_gloss: And not only do they gain to feast thus splendidly, but they also lead away hands filled with costly gifts, and they learn from us that it is more profitable to pursue and practice such things than the virtues. But if a poor man should stand before us, scarcely even speaking because of hunger, we turn away from the one of the same race, we loathe him, we run off with haste, as if fearing lest we share in his very misfortune by walking more slowly. And if he should bow to the ground, ashamed of his calamity, we say that he is a worker of hypocrisy; but if he should look at us with boldness because of the heavy goad of hunger, we call him shameless and violent. And if he should happen to be covered with sound garments, someone having given them, we drive him away as insatiable, and we swear that he pretends poverty; but if he should be covered with rotten rags, we chase him away again as stinking, and neither by mixing the name of the Creator into his supplications, nor by adjuring us continually that we not fall into such sufferings, can he bend our merciless choice. For these reasons I suspect the fire to be heavier than hell, more than that rich man did. If then the occasion allowed, and sufficient power were present, I would have gone through all the things concerning that man, as the Book showed, and rendered the work of the words; but now it is time to release you who are weary. But you yourselves, if we have omitted anything through weakness of thought and tongue, fashioning it for yourselves, apply it like medicines to the wounds of your souls. For give to a wise man an occasion, and he will be wiser, says the Scripture. And God is able to make every grace abound to you, so that, having all sufficiency in everything always, you may abound in every good work. But now, as you see, the word having been brought down to harbor for us, some brothers lead it back again to the course of counsel, bidding us not to run past the things marvelously worked yesterday by the Master, nor to silence the trophy which the Savior set up against the madness of the devil, but to give you an occasion for the leapings of hymn-singing. For again, as you know, the devil displayed his own madness against us, and arming himself with flame of fire, he marched against the sanctuaries of the church. But again the common mother conquered, and turned the device back upon the enemy, and nothing was his except to publicize his hatred. Grace blew against the enemy's onsets; the temple remained unharmed. The storm brought by the enemy was not strong enough to shake the rock on which Christ built the fold of his own flock. He who long ago quenched the furnace in Babylon was stationed now with us. How do you think the devil groans today, not having enjoyed the attempt in the way he wished? For the hostile one kindled a pyre near the church, in order to harm our prosperity; and the flame, fanned from every side by his violent blasts, poured over the things lying beneath it, and devoured the air nearby, compelled to touch the sanctuaries, and dragging us down to share in the calamity. But the Savior made it flow upon the one who kindled it, and commanded his madness to contract again into himself.

choices.english: the one of the same race
choices.why: Literal rendering of the compound adjective, emphasizing shared human nature, which Basil uses to heighten the shame of rejection.
Literal sense of κέντρον as a sharp instrument of compulsion, matching the image of hunger driving the poor man to boldness.
The infinitive clause has the poor man as subject, not the speakers; the accusation is that the beggar is faking his poverty.
First person singular verb, Basil indicting himself along with the congregation; the suspicion is his own.
Refers to the recent fire (ἐμπρησμός) just experienced, not hell; Basil says this fire's judgment is heavier than hell was for the rich man.
Literal rendering of προαίρεσις as deliberate choice or resolve, emphasizing the willful hardness of the hearers.

pass_b_english: And they do not gain only the brilliant feasting itself. They also go away with their hands filled with costly gifts, and they learn from us that it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them, rather than the virtues. But if a poor man should stand before us, barely able to speak from hunger, we turn away from the one of the same race, we loathe him, we run off in haste, as if afraid that by walking too slowly we might share in his very misfortune. And if he should bow his head to the ground, ashamed of his calamity, we say he is a worker of hypocrisy. But if he should look at us boldly because of the heavy goad of hunger, we call him shameless and violent. And if he happens to be covered with sound clothing someone has given him, we drive him away as insatiable, and we swear that he pretends poverty. But if he is covered with rotten rags, we chase him off again as stinking. And neither by mixing the name of his Creator into his supplications, nor by constantly adjuring us that we may not fall into such sufferings, can he bend our merciless choice. For these reasons I suspect the fire of hell will be heavier for us than it was for that rich man. Now if the occasion allowed and sufficient strength were present, I would have gone through everything concerning that man, as the Book has shown, and paid you the full work of my words. But now it is time to release you who are weary. And you yourselves, if we have omitted anything through weakness of thought and tongue, fashion it for yourselves and apply it like medicines to the wounds of your souls. For give an opportunity to a wise man, and he will be wiser, says the Scripture (Proverbs 9:9). And God is able to make every grace abound to you, so that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work (2 Corinthians 9:8). But now, as you see, the word has already been brought down to harbor for us, and some brothers are leading it back again to the course of counsel, bidding us not to pass over what was wondrously done yesterday by the Master, nor to keep silent about the trophy that the Savior set up against the devil's madness, but to give you an occasion for the leaping of hymns. For again, as you know, the devil displayed his own madness against us, and arming himself with a flame of fire, he marched against the folds of the church. But again our common mother conquered, and turned the enemy's device back upon him, and nothing remained to him except to make his hatred public. Grace blew against the enemy's blasts. The temple remained untouched. The storm brought by the enemy was not strong enough to shake the rock on which Christ built the sheepfold of his own flock. He who long ago quenched the furnace in Babylon was stationed with us now as well (Daniel 3:49-50). How do you think the devil groans today, not having enjoyed the attempt on which he had set his desire? For the hostile one kindled a pyre next to the church, to damage our prosperity. And the flame, fanned from every side by his violent blasts, poured over what lay beneath it and fed on the air nearby, compelled to touch the sacred precincts and dragging us down into a share of the calamity. But the Savior made it flow back upon the one who kindled it, and commanded his madness to contract again upon himself.

problems.quote: not having enjoyed the outcome of the attempt he desired
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἀπολαύσας ἐφ' ᾧπερ ἠβουλήθη τῆς ἐγχειρήσεως
problems.why: ἐφ' ᾧπερ = 'in which' (the attempt), not 'the outcome of'. He did not get to enjoy the attempt itself.
problems.fix: not having enjoyed the attempt on which he set his desire
problems.ruling: ἐφ' ᾧπερ = 'in which' (the attempt), not 'outcome'. Meaning changed: devil didn't enjoy the attempt itself.

problems.quote: pursuing and practicing such things is more profitable than the virtues
problems.source_quote: λυσιτελεῖ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα μετιέναι καὶ πράττειν αὐτοῖς
problems.why: Sense reversed: Greek says pursuing virtues is more profitable than such things, not vice versa.
problems.fix: that pursuing and practicing virtues is more profitable than such things
problems.ruling: λυσιτελεῖ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα = 'such things more profitable than virtues.' English reverses this, saying virtues are more profitable.

edits.old: not having enjoyed the outcome of the attempt he desired
edits.new: not having enjoyed the attempt on which he had set his desire

edits.old: pursuing and practicing such things is more profitable than the virtues
edits.new: pursuing and practicing the virtues is more profitable than such things

fixed: Corrected 'not having enjoyed the outcome of the attempt he desired' to 'not having enjoyed the attempt on which he had set his desire': the Greek ἐφ' ᾧπερ means 'in which' referring to the attempt itself, not its outcome.

Corrected 'pursuing and practicing such things is more profitable than the virtues' to 'pursuing and practicing the virtues is more profitable than such things': the Greek λυσιτελεῖ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα μετιέναι means it is more profitable to pursue the virtues than such things.

problems.quote: I suspect the fire is heavier than hell was for that rich man
problems.source_quote: Διὰ ταῦτα ὑφορῶμαι βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος
problems.why: Misreads ὑφορῶμαι: 'I suspect' should be 'I fear/apprehend'; misreads syntax: 'the fire is heavier than hell was for that rich man' should be 'the fire [will be] heavier for them than hell was for that rich man'.
problems.fix: For these reasons I fear the fire will be heavier for them than hell was for that rich man.

problems.quote: And they learn from us that pursuing and practicing the virtues is more profitable than such things
problems.source_quote: μανθάνουσι παρ' ἡμῶν, ὅτι λυσιτελεῖ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα μετιέναι καὶ πράττειν αὐτοῖς
problems.why: Source says 'they learn from us that it is more profitable to pursue such things and to practice them with virtues' — τῶν ἀρετῶν is genitive of association 'with virtues', not 'the virtues' as the object of pursuing.
problems.fix: they learn from us that it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them with virtues
problems.ruling: τῶν ἀρετῶν is genitive, not accusative: 'with virtues' or 'rather than virtues', not 'the virtues' as object.

edits.old: I suspect the fire is heavier than hell was for that rich man
edits.new: I fear the fire will be heavier for them than hell was for that rich man

edits.old: they learn from us that pursuing and practicing the virtues is more profitable than such things
edits.new: they learn from us that it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them with virtues

fixed: ὑφορῶμαι means 'I fear/apprehend', not 'I suspect'; the syntax makes the fire heavier for 'them' (the unmerciful) than hell was for the rich man.
τῶν ἀρετῶν is genitive of association ('with virtues'), not the object of pursuing; the source says it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them with virtues.

problems.why: Greek says 'do/practice them' (the things), not 'with virtues'; virtues are the object of pursuing, not instrument.
problems.fix: pursue such things and practice them, rather than virtues

problems.quote: I fear the fire will be heavier for them than hell was for that rich man
problems.source_quote: ὑφορῶμαι βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος
problems.why: Greek says 'I suspect/fear the fire [will be] heavier than hell for that rich man'—comparing the fire to hell for the rich man, not 'for them' vs 'for that rich man'. The fire (of judgment) will be heavier than hell was for the rich man.
problems.fix: I suspect the fire will be heavier than hell was for that rich man

problems.quote: than hell was for that rich man
problems.source_quote: βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος
problems.why: Full source: 'I fear the fire heavier than Gehenna than that rich man.' The rich man is compared to the fire's heaviness, not hell's.
problems.fix: I fear the fire will be heavier for them than that rich man was for hell
problems.ruling: Greek βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος means 'the fire heavier than Gehenna than that rich man [was]'; English 'heavier for them than hell was for that rich man' misconstructs the comparison structure.

problems.why: Greek 'sēkoi' means 'folds/enclosures/dwellings', especially of sheep; 'sanctuaries' is too grand and misses the sheepfold imagery that continues with 'mandra' below.
problems.ruling: σηκοῖς = folds/enclosures, often sheepfolds; 'sanctuaries' loses sheepfold imagery linking to μάνδραν below.

edits.old: it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them with virtues
edits.new: it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them, rather than the virtues

edits.old: I fear the fire will be heavier for them than hell was for that rich man
edits.new: I suspect the fire will be heavier than hell was for that rich man

fixed: Corrected 'practice them with virtues' to 'practice them, rather than the virtues' because the Greek πράττειν αὐτοῖς means 'practice them' (the things), and the comparison is between such things and the virtues.

Corrected 'I fear the fire will be heavier for them than hell was for that rich man' to 'I suspect the fire will be heavier than hell was for that rich man' because the Greek ὑφορῶμαι βαρύτερον τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ ἤπερ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πλούσιος compares the fire to hell for that rich man, not 'for them' versus 'for that rich man'.
Corrected 'sanctuaries of the church' to 'folds of the church' because the Greek σηκοῖς means 'folds/enclosures', continuing the sheepfold imagery with μάνδρα below.

fixed.quote: I suspect the fire will be heavier than hell was for that rich man
fixed.fix: I suspect the fire of hell will be heavier for us than it was for that rich man
fixed.note: τῆς γεέννης τὸ πῦρ means 'the fire of hell', and the comparison is with what the rich man suffered; the English wrongly sets the fire against hell itself.

dismissed.quote: it is more profitable to pursue such things and practice them, rather than the virtues
dismissed.why: Greek says pursuing virtues is more profitable; English reverses to say pursuing gifts is more profitable.
dismissed.note: μᾶλλον τῶν ἀρετῶν means 'rather than the virtues' and τὰ τοιαῦτα is the object of 'pursue', so the English is correct; the proposed fix would reverse the meaning.

dismissed.quote: we swear that he pretends poverty
dismissed.why: Source means 'we swear he is pretending poverty'; English could read as swearing to pretend poverty ourselves.
dismissed.note: 'We swear that he pretends poverty' is clear in context and faithful to the Greek.
